Article Title: Meta's highest-paid employee Alexandr Wang can't stop making fun of Google, says who is ...
Article Text:
Meta AI head

The benchmark behind Alexandr Wang’s dig at Google

Where the gains came from

The cost advantage

Alexandr Wang, Meta’s chief AI officer and highest-paid employee recently took a jab at Google ’s Gemini after a benchmark data shoed Meta’s latest AU model climbing near the very top of the industry rankings. In a post shared on social media platform X (formerly known as Twitter) Wang wrote, “I really hate to say it, but… gemini who? 🚀💨” alongside a performance chart showing Meta’s Muse Spark 1.3 surpassing several Gemini variants on the Artificial Analysis Intelligence Index. According to Artificial Analysis, Muse Spark 1.3 scored 62 points, placing it behind only Anthropic’s Claude Fable 5.1 (66) and Claude Opus 5 (63). The model outperformed Google’s Gemini 1.5 Pro and Gemini 1.5 Flash, which scored 61 and 53 respectively.Wang's comment was posted in response to a thread from Artificial Analysis announcing that Meta had released Muse Spark 1.3, the company's fourth Muse Spark model release in just five months. According to the benchmark firm, Muse Spark 1.3 (max) — currently in limited preview for Meta's partners — scored 62 on the Artificial Analysis Intelligence Index, trailing only Claude Fable 5.1 and Claude Opus 5 in their top configurations.The publicly available variant, Muse Spark 1.3 (xhigh), scored 61 on the same index, putting it in a tie with GPT-5.6 Sol (max), Grok 4.6 (high), and Claude Opus 5 (high). That score represents a 4-point jump from Muse Spark 1.2's score of 57 in August, and an 8-point gain over Muse Spark 1.1's score of 53 in July. It landed just behind Claude Fable 5.1 (max, 66), Claude Opus 5 (max, 63), and Claude Fable 5 (max, 62).According to Artificial Analysis, both new Muse Spark variants improved primarily in two areas: agentic task performance and scientific reasoning.On agentic work, Muse Spark 1.3 (xhigh) posted a 12-point gain over Muse Spark 1.2 on the Tau3-Bench Banking evaluation, rising from 35% to 47%, along with a 5-point gain on Terminal-Bench 2.1 (80% to 85%) and a jump in GDPval-AA v2 Elo rating from 1,615 to 1,709. The limited-preview Muse Spark 1.3 (max) variant pushed even further, reaching 52% on Tau3-Bench Banking — the highest score of any model on that specific benchmark — and a GDPval-AA v2 Elo of 1,754. Artificial Analysis noted that Muse Spark 1.3 (max) achieves these higher scores in part by using significantly more reasoning tokens than the xhigh variant, reasoning 62% more on GDPval-AA v2 and 28% more on Tau3-Bench Banking.On scientific reasoning, the standout gain came on CritPt, where the xhigh variant improved 8 points over Muse Spark 1.2, from 18% to 26%. GPQA Diamond rose 4 points, from 90% to 94%, while Humanity's Last Exam and SciCode each posted more modest 2-to-3-point gains.Beyond performance, Muse Spark 1.3 also demonstrated efficiency. The xhigh variant costs about $0.55 per task, significantly lower than GPT‑5.6 Sol and Grok 4.6, which cost nearly double. Analysts noted this places Muse Spark on the “Pareto frontier” for intelligence versus cost, making it one of the most competitive models in terms of value.For those unaware, Meta has released four Muse Spark models in just five months, underscoring its aggressive push in frontier AI.
Article Summary: Alexandr Wang, Meta’s chief AI officer and highest-paid employee, recently took a jab at Google ’s Gemini. Wang wrote, “I really hate to say it, but… gemini who? 🚀💨” alongside a performance chart showing Meta's Muse Spark 1.3 surpassing several Gemini variants on the Artificial Analysis Intelligence Index. According to the benchmark firm, Muse Spark1.3 (max) — currently in limited preview for Meta's partners — scored 62.

Article Title: Netflix unveils ‘VOID’, an AI model that can change a movie plot
Article Text:
Netflix

How Netflix VOID works







Netflix has unveiled an AI model that can alter the scene. While this is nothing new, Netflix’s model not just remove objects from video, it understands what should happen next, essentially altering the causality. Most object-removal technology leaves a gap where something used to be and/ or fills it with a plausible-looking background. VOID goes a step further: after erasing an object from a scene, it calculates how the surrounding environment should realistically respond to its absence, and in the process it adjusts the behaviour of other elements in the frame accordingly.The model, called VOID, is a vision-language system designed to edit video footage with a level of contextual awareness that sets it apart from several existing tools.For example, imagine this scenario: A movie director has just wrapped up a multi-million dollar action sequence where the star drives straight into a fiery, head-on collision. The cars explode, debris scatters, and the scene is a wrap.But suddenly, there is request to change the scene: The character survives and drive off into the sunset instead. This would mean costly reshoots or millions spent on computer-generated graphics.Netflix’s VOID can alter the scene and digitally erase the collision, the second vehicle, the smoke, and the flying debris. It will then generate new, realistic footage of pristine pavement, making it look as though the main character simply drove down an empty, peaceful road.The AI’s ‘magic’ lies in its grasp of real-world physics. Let us understand this by a different example. If a video shows a person jumping into a pool and splashing water onto the deck, VOID can completely erase the person. It will then intelligently alter the water and the wet concrete, leaving behind a perfectly still, undisturbed pool as if nobody had ever jumped in.“To train the model, we generate a new paired dataset of counterfactual object removals using Kubric and HUMOTO, where removing an object requires altering downstream physical interactions. During inference, a vision-language model identifies regions of the scene affected by the removed object. These regions are then used to guide a video diffusion model that generates physically consistent counterfactual outcomes,” Netflix said.“Experiments on both synthetic and real data show that our approach better preserves consistent scene dynamics after object removal compared to prior video object removal methods,” the company added.Netflix isn’t keeping this powerful tool locked behind studio doors, and made the VOID model available to the public on the AI platform Hugging Face, allowing anyone to download and use it.While there are already several video-altering tools on the market, such as Runway, DiffuEraser, and ProPainter, the Netflix team claims VOID is vastly superior, as per The Register.
Article Summary: Netflix has unveiled an AI model that can alter the scene. While this is nothing new, Netflix’s model not just remove objects from video, it understands what should happen next, essentially altering the causality. The model, called VOID, is a vision-language system designed to edit video footage with a level of contextual awareness.

Article Title: FDA suspends EatClub Brands' food licence over violations in Mumbai; MOJO Pizza, BOX8 among those hit
Article Text:
Mumbai's Food and Drug Administration has suspended several food licences.





MUMBAI: The Food and Drug Administration (FDA) has suspended the food licence of EatClub Brands in Goregaon, which operates brands like MOJO Pizza, BOX8, ZAZA Mughal Biryani, Itminaan Matka Biryani, LeanCrust Pizza, and WeFit. The company runs cloud kitchens and functions on a delivery-only model.At EatClub's facility in Royal Palms, Goregaon, inspectors found a lack of storage facilities for raw ingredients and chemicals, poor pest control, unauthorised sales of ice cream and carbonated beverages, and workers operating without basic safety gear.In Kurla, Rani Creators Consultant and Service Providers had its food licence suspended as inspections showed an active rodent and pest infestation, stagnant water pooling on broken flooring, and high-risk raw meats stored uncovered next to decaying produce. It did not maintain cooking temperature logs and relied on blackened, degraded frying oil.Two bakeries in Chembur, Goodluck Bakery & Stores and Ashfaque Bakery, fell far short of compliance benchmarks.
Article Summary: Mumbai's Food and Drug Administration has suspended several food licences. Inspectors found a lack of storage facilities for raw ingredients and chemicals. Two bakeries in Chembur, Goodluck Bakery & Stores and Ashfaque Bakery, fell far short of compliance benchmarks.

Article Title: Fraudster uses Raigad SP’s WhatsApp display photo to dupe police staff, seeks Rs 50,000
Article Text:
A cyber fraudster impersonated Raigad SP on WhatsApp, targeting police personnel for money transfers, but the scam attempt was foiled. (AI-generated image)





NAVI MUMBAI: Raigad Cyber Police have registered a case against an unidentified fraudster who allegedly used the WhatsApp Display Picture (DP) of Raigad Superintendent of Police (SP) Anchal Dalal to deceive several police personnel into transferring money.On Thursday, the fraudster sent a message to Raigad SP's reader, PSI Siddheshwar Murkute, asking him to transfer money urgently. Murkute immediately realised that it was a modus operandi commonly used by cyber scammers, as the WhatsApp message was sent from an international number that was not saved in his mobile phone.Thereafter, PSI Murkute learnt that the same scammer had sent similar messages to several Raigad police personnel. Fortunately, no one fell prey to the fraud, as the police personnel were aware of this modus operandi used by cyber fraudsters.Subsequently, PSI Murkute registered an FIR against the unidentified accused under the relevant section of the BNS for the offence of cheating by personation.The complainant, PSI Murkute, said, "I had received the WhatsApp message from an international number and the DP was of Raigad SP Anchal Dalal.The message read, 'I am in a meeting and my mobile is switched off. Immediately transfer Rs 50,000 to my bank account.' I knew the message sender was a scammer. I deliberately replied asking for the bank account number by pretending to send the money. As I received the bank account number from the scammer, it will be useful for the cyber police team to trace the bank account holder. "PSI Murkute added, "One police officer had received a WhatsApp message from the same international number asking to transfer Rs 2,000 by impersonating SP madam and claiming that it was required for filling diesel in the car, and that her mobile battery had drained and she was unable to pay online at the fuel station."API Amol Jadhav of Raigad Cyber Police said, "The cyber scammers use VPNs (Virtual Private Networks) to mask their identity. However, the Internet Protocol (IP) address of the WhatsApp number used by the accused will be obtained to trace the location, and the accused will soon be behind bars."
Article Summary: A cyber fraudster impersonated Raigad SP on WhatsApp, targeting police personnel for money transfers. Fortunately, no one fell prey to the fraud, as the police personnel were aware of this modus operandi used by cyber fraudsters. One police officer received a WhatsApp message from the same international number asking to transfer Rs 2,000 by impersonating SP madam.

Article Title: In 2007, American Peace Corps volunteer Laura Kutner began collecting plastic bottles in Granados; by 2009, they formed 2 schoolrooms and inspired 10 more schools
Article Text:
Representation of a school built with thousands of discarded plastic bottles, showcasing an innovative approach to turning waste into useful building materials. Image Credits: ChatGPT.

From litter to building material

What the bottles could actually do

Plastic bottles landfill. Image credits: Wikimedia Commons

An idea that travelled beyond Granados

A discarded plastic bottle is usually treated as a piece of waste, but in Granados, Guatemala, thousands of them became part of a school. When American Peace Corps volunteer Laura Kutner arrived in the mountainous community in 2007, she encountered both a shortage of classroom space and a persistent waste problem. Two unfinished classrooms already had metal frames and roofs, but there was not enough money to complete the walls. Kutner eventually found a way to turn the rubbish around the community into a construction material.According to Smithsonian Magazine, Granados, in Guatemala's Baja Verapaz region, had limited waste-disposal options, and rubbish frequently accumulated around the community. Kutner noticed the problem while working with local students and began considering whether some of that waste could be put to practical use. The idea came while she was sitting with students and drinking from a plastic bottle. She realised that the bottle was roughly the same width as the metal framing of the unfinished classrooms. Kutner had also encountered examples from elsewhere in Latin America where plastic bottles packed with waste were being used as building blocks.With the support of local engineers, she began adapting the approach for the school. The process was simple, but labour-intensive. Students and residents collected discarded plastic bottles, cleaned them and packed them tightly with inorganic waste such as plastic bags, wrappers and aluminium packaging. Paper and cardboard were excluded because they could decompose inside the bottles. The resulting "eco-bricks" were then placed inside metal frames and enclosed with chicken wire before the walls were covered with concrete.Kutner and school principal Reyna Ortiz organised workshops to explain how the bottles had to be prepared. Students were encouraged to collect and fill bottles themselves, and as the project required more material, volunteers also travelled to neighbouring communities to collect additional bottles and waste. What began as a way to complete two unfinished classrooms consequently expanded into a broader community clean-up effort. Construction of the walls began in February 2009. Kutner was later transferred to San Miguel Dueñas, but continued travelling back to Granados as the project neared completion. By October that year, the wall was finished, forming part of the two-room school.The Granados project was more than an unusual recycling exercise. It demonstrated how a material with little immediate value could be incorporated into a low-cost construction system when conventional building materials were difficult to afford. Research published in Materials & Design later examined the physical properties of PET bottle eco-bricks made by packing waste plastic into bottles. Laboratory tests found that their mechanical strength was closely related to how heavily the bottles were packed, while the researchers also identified potential benefits in sound insulation and light transmission. The study concluded that such eco-bricks could have construction applications, although their suitability depends on how they are manufactured and where they are used. This is important because a plastic bottle does not automatically become a replacement for a concrete block simply because it is tightly packed with rubbish.The most lasting part of the project was perhaps what happened after the classrooms were completed. Kutner continued sharing the construction method, while other volunteers and communities became interested in the approach. Smithsonian reported that 10 additional schools had been built in Guatemala using the plastic-bottle technique. The Peace Corps also documented how the project encouraged communities to think differently about waste. Instead of treating discarded bottles and wrappers solely as rubbish, residents could collect, sort and repurpose some of that material. The project therefore connected two local problems, unfinished school construction and unmanaged waste, through a single community effort.According to a field report published in Children, Youth and Environments , Laura Kutner’s classroom project in Granados, Guatemala, involved children and young people in every stage, from collecting waste to constructing the classrooms. She highlighted hands-on learning, teamwork, creativity and community participation as key to creating more sustainable projects. The Granados classrooms were completed in 2009 and are now about 17 years old. However, the available reports do not provide a recent assessment of their condition or long-term performance.The project showed something more practical: even a material regarded as worthless can become useful when a community has the need, organisation and technical guidance to put it to another purpose. In Granados, thousands of bottles that might otherwise have remained scattered around the town instead became part of a school where children could learn. And the method did not remain confined to those two classrooms. It became an example that other communities in Guatemala chose to adapt, turning a small local experiment into a much wider idea.
Article Summary: American Peace Corps volunteer Laura Kutner used plastic bottles to build a school in Granados, Guatemala. Students and residents collected discarded plastic bottles, cleaned them and packed them tightly with inorganic waste such as plastic bags, wrappers and aluminium packaging. Paper and cardboard were excluded because they could decompose inside the bottles. The resulting "eco- bricks" were then placed inside metal frames and enclosed with chicken wire.

Article Title: In 2017, USGS injected 13.5 liters of red dye into Ohio’s Sandusky River during a grass carp spawning event; downstream stations measured dye movement
Article Text:
An AI-generated image showing researchers releasing red tracer dye into Ohio’s Sandusky River to measure how material drifting in the current moves downstream during grass carp spawning research. Credits - Google Gemini

Why a river needed to be dyed at all

Watching red water pass a string of stations

An AI-generated image showing scientists monitoring the Sandusky River downstream after a red dye tracer was released to study water movement and help model the drift of grass carp eggs. Credits - ChatGPT

Turning drift times into a map of where carp spawn

Some invasive species are easy to track because they leave visible damage behind, such as stripped vegetation or a collapsed food web that points investigators to the culprit. Grass carp are harder to track because they spawn by releasing eggs directly into moving water rather than building a nest researchers can easily locate and observe. Scientists working on Ohio's Sandusky River needed a way around that problem. On 11 July 2017, USGS researchers injected 13.5 litres of Rhodamine WT dye into the Sandusky River at the Tiffin Road bridge crossing. The timing was deliberate. A grass carp spawning event was already underway downstream, and scientists from the US Geological Survey wanted to know how far and how fast a fish egg would drift once it entered the water. Those measurements could then be used to improve models of where grass carp eggs were likely to have originated.Grass carp are not native to the Sandusky River or anywhere in the Great Lakes basin. The species was brought to the United States in the 1960s to control aquatic vegetation, and escaped populations later established themselves in the Mississippi River system before spreading toward Lake Erie.Spawning was first confirmed in the Sandusky River in 2015, when researchers collected fertilised eggs drifting downstream, and further surveys in the years that followed documented repeated spawning events in the same stretch of river. That confirmation mattered because fertilised grass carp eggs behave in a specific way once they are released. Rather than sinking or sticking to the riverbed, they remain suspended in the current as they drift and develop, so their fate depends largely on how the water is moving. That single fact, that eggs travel much like any other object caught in the current, is what made a dye tracer study worth running in the first place.Rhodamine WT, the dye used in the study, is a bright red compound that fluoresces under the right light and can be measured at very low concentrations, making it useful for tracing how quickly water moves through a river system. According to a USGS data release, the dye was injected near the Tiffin Road bridge crossing, and its concentration was then recorded at fixed monitoring stations downstream over the following two days, alongside water velocity and discharge readings taken from survey boats stationed on the river. Because the dye moved with the river current, the data showed how quickly material entering the river near a suspected spawning site would reach each downstream sampling point and how that timing varied with flow. Matching the dye data against the eggs researchers found in their nets was the next step, and it is where the study's value emerged.Ichthyoplankton nets at multiple sites along the lower Sandusky River had already collected thousands of grass carp eggs on several dates in 2017. Pairing that catch data with the dye study allowed scientists to work backward from where an egg was caught to roughly where and when it was spawned. A related USGS publication describes using drift modelling to estimate a likely spawning location several kilometres downstream of Ballville Dam. In June 2018, researchers collected fertilised eggs and adult grass carp within that model-predicted spawning area, confirming the location and validating the modelling approach. The dye tracer study filled that gap by using coloured water and careful timing. The approach has since become a template for tracking other river-spawning species whose eggs, like grass carp eggs, drift rather than stay put.
Article Summary: US Geological Survey researchers injected 13.5 litres of Rhodamine WT dye into the Sandusky River at the Tiffin Road bridge crossing. A grass carp spawning event was already underway downstream, and scientists from the US Geological Survey wanted to know how far and how fast a fish egg would drift once it entered the water.

Article Title: In 2021, South Carolina sank a retired 250-foot barge off Edisto Island; its water tower and containers now give snapper and grouper cave-like shelter
Article Text:
An AI generated image showing underwater view of a commercial barge moving through a river, illustrating the hidden activity and water movement beneath the surface. Credits - Google Gemini

A partnership behind the scrap pile

Why shape matters more than size to a fish

Swamp Sculpture - Edisto Island. Credits - Wikimedia Commons

A layered habitat built over decades

Much of South Carolina’s seafloor is flat and sandy, offering little shelter for fish along the coast. For decades, the state’s wildlife managers have tried to change that by sinking retired ships, vehicles and construction debris to give marine life places to cling to and hide. One of their more elaborate efforts came in September 2021, when a 250-foot decommissioned barge was towed about 10 nautical miles off Edisto Island and deliberately sunk. On its deck were sections of a dismantled municipal water tower, a dozen shipping containers with holes cut through their steel walls, and a life-sized concrete sculpture of a great white shark. It took approximately two hours for the barge to disappear beneath the waves. Five years later, the structure remains part of the Edisto 60-foot artificial reef, where its containers and water-tower sections provide the varied shelter the project was designed to create for marine lifeThe project was led by the South Carolina Department of Natural Resources, whose artificial reef programme has spent decades building habitat along a coastline short of hard, rocky seafloor. According to SCDNR , the barge and its cargo were contributed through a partnership with the Coastal Conservation Association of South Carolina and Sea Hunt Boat Company, which together funded half the cost of the barge and its tow to the reef site. The water tower sections came from Mount Pleasant, which had recently demolished an old municipal tank and donated the steel instead of scrapping it. For the Coastal Conservation Association, the Edisto deployment marked its fifteenth reef contribution in the state, part of a longer-running effort to keep adding material to South Carolina's permitted reef sites.Robert Martore, the programme’s long-time head, explained that the key factor was shelter, not size.According to the South Carolina Department of Natural Resources, the open spaces inside the shipping containers create a cave-like interior that larger species such as snapper and grouper prefer, while the flatter pieces of the water tower provide low-relief refuge for smaller and juvenile fish. That mix of structure sizes is deliberate. A stretch of open sand offers almost nothing for a young fish to hide behind, so even modest variation in height and enclosure can draw in a wider range of species than a single uniform shape would. That same logic, giving fish a reason to stay rather than simply pass through, is the entire premise behind building artificial reefs at all.The barge did not create a reef so much as add to an existing one. Known as the Edisto 60-foot reef, or PA 30, the site lies about 10 nautical miles offshore and had already received more than 20 structures before 2021, including a large ship, decommissioned military vehicles and rubble salvaged from the old Cooper River Bridge. According to NOAA Fisheries , artificial reefs work by providing new or enhanced hard-bottom habitat in areas that would otherwise be habitat-limited, giving space for organisms to colonise quickly and offering juvenile fish more places to shelter from predators. Along much of South Carolina's coast, where the natural seafloor is largely flat and sandy, that kind of added structure can make an outsized difference to how much marine life an area supports.For anglers and divers, the appeal is immediate. A reef with this variety of structure can provide habitat for snapper, grouper and other reef-associated species, turning otherwise open seafloor into a more complex fishing and diving site. Species such as red snapper and gag grouper are slow to mature and tend to stay close to the structure they settle near, which is why fisheries managers pay close attention to where new reef material is placed. There is also a concrete shark at one end of the wreck, a detail that has nothing to do with fish biology. Programme staff built the sculpture themselves as something divers would enjoy photographing, a small acknowledgement that an artificial reef is meant to be visited as well as inhabited.
Article Summary: South Carolina's artificial reef programme has spent decades building habitat along a coastline short of hard, rocky seafloor. One of their more elaborate efforts came in September 2021, when a 250-foot decommissioned barge was towed about 10 nautical miles off Edisto Island and deliberately sunk. On its deck were sections of a dismantled municipal water tower, a dozen shipping containers with holes cut through their steel walls, and a life-sized concrete shark.

Article Title: A 5,000-acre Wyoming ranch was bought by conservationists in the 1990s; instead of ending ranching, they kept cattle grazing to protect the ecosystem
Article Text:
Image: Timothy Rockhold

How a Wyoming ranch proved cattle grazing could save an ecosystem, not destroy it

Why grazing stayed part of the plan

Cattle at Red Canyon Ranch (Image: Chuck Diggins)

Balancing wildlife, water, and working land

A model that still shapes conservation today

When conservationists bought a Wyoming cattle ranch in the 1990s, most people assumed the herds would disappear. Instead, they discovered something surprising: keeping cattle on the land, managed carefully, could actually protect it. This is the story of Red Canyon Ranch near Lander, Wyoming, purchased by The Nature Conservancy as an experiment in coexistence between ranching and wildlife. Rather than retiring the pastures, the organisation kept roughly 600 head of cattle grazing across the property, using science to test whether livestock and native ecosystems could genuinely thrive together. Decades later, the ranch stands as a working case study in adaptive land management, one that continues to shape how conservation groups across the American West think about grazing, biodiversity, and the future of working lands.In the early 1990s, The Nature Conservancy acquired Red Canyon Ranch, a roughly 35,000-acre spread near Lander, Wyoming, made up of about 5,000 deeded acres alongside tens of thousands of leased federal acres. The purchase was unusual for its time. Rather than converting the property into an untouched nature preserve, the organization chose to keep it operating as a working cattle ranch. This decision reflected a broader shift within the conservation world during the era, one that questioned whether removing all human activity was truly the best path to protecting fragile landscapes, or whether carefully managed use could sometimes do the job just as well.Cattle didn't stay on Red Canyon Ranch out of sentiment, the reasoning was ecological. For thousands of years, grazing animals had shaped Wyoming's sagebrush steppe and grasslands, starting with bison and other native herbivores that roamed the land long before ranching existed. Pull large grazers out entirely, and you don't necessarily get a healthier landscape; you risk disrupting processes the ecosystem has come to depend on. So the Conservancy took a different route: using cattle to stand in for that lost grazing pressure, moving herds through rotational and adaptive patterns designed to echo how wild grazers once used the land. This approach aimed to maintain healthy grasslands, support diverse plant communities, and avoid the overgrazing that had damaged other Western rangelands throughout the twentieth century.However, the rationale for cattle grazing at the Red Canyon Ranch was based on ecology, not emotions. Large grazers have been a part of the sagebrush steppe and grasslands of Wyoming for thousands of years, first in the form of bison and other native herbivores. Complete elimination of grazing from the area, experts argued, would not be a restoration but an interference into the natural processes. Hence, The Conservancy used cattle to emulate the historical pattern of grazing with the use of rotational and adaptive grazing techniques. The ongoing presence of a working herd meant researchers could gather real, long-term data on how grazing intensity and timing affected the broader ecosystem.Red Canyon Ranch helped popularize a strategy now used on conservation properties across the West: keeping agriculture and biodiversity goals aligned rather than treating them as opposites. The approach has since informed similar projects on other working ranches, where conservation groups partner with ranchers instead of buying them out entirely. It hasn't been without debate, since some critics argue that any grazing carries ecological costs compared with fully rested land. Still, the ranch's decades-long track record offers real evidence that thoughtfully managed livestock operations can coexist with wildlife conservation, offering a template for balancing food production, rural livelihoods, and ecosystem health.
Article Summary: Red Canyon Ranch near Lander, Wyoming, was purchased by The Nature Conservancy in the 1990s. Rather than retiring the pastures, the organisation kept roughly 600 head of cattle grazing across the property. The ranch stands as a working case study in adaptive land management, one that continues to shape how conservation groups across the American West think about grazing.

Article Title: ChatGPT is first AI chatbot to face tougher EU rules
Article Text:
ChatGPT is first AI chatbot to face tougher EU rules﻿

ChatGPT will have to comply with tougher safety rules after the EU added it Monday to a list of digital services subject to greater legal scrutiny, a first for an AI chatbot.Brussels also designated Reddit and Roblox as “very large” online platforms, a label that comes with additional obligations and oversight. “ChatGPT, Reddit and Roblox will now be held to a higher standard of scrutiny and accountability in the EU, in line with their large impact on our citizens and society,” EU technology chief Henna Virkkunen said.The designation applies to platforms and search engines with over 45 million monthly active users in the 27-nation bloc, a threshold the three platforms reported meeting, the commission said. The three now have four months to comply with additional obligations under the Digital Services Act, a content law the EU has deployed to rein in Big Tech.

Article Title: Meet Yanin ‘Proud’, a 17-year-old Thai student who built artificial hornbill nests from recycled plastic and won two global conservation awards
Article Text:
Yanin (Proud) Tangkaravakoon. Image Credit: The Nation

How did this 17-year-old Thai student turn recycled plastic into artificial hornbill nests

,

The nest design was developed to solve the weaknesses of older options

Hornbill showing interest in the artificial nest. Image Credit: The Earth Prize

The artificial nests are already giving hornbills new breeding opportunities

Why does education remain an important part of Homes for Hornbills

At just 17, Thai student Yanin ‘Proud’ Tangkaravakoon has turned a concern for endangered hornbills into a unique conservation project that gives discarded waste plastic a new purpose. Her initiative, ‘Homes for Hornbills’ creates artificial nests designed to provide breeding spaces for hornbills as natural tree cavities become harder to find. The project has now earned her two major international honours, including recognition from ‘The Earth Prize’ and National Geographic’s ‘Slingshot Challenge.’ According to Khaosod English, the project combines wildlife conservation, recycled materials and community involvement to address the declining populations of hornbills in Thailand. The Nation reported that the nests have been developed with attention to the birds’ behaviour, safety and the environmental conditions they face. What began with a young student’s fascination with these distinctive birds has grown into a practical conservation effort with encouraging early results. The initiative shows how a simple idea can bring together young people, local communities and practical conservation to create new possibilities for threatened wildlife.According to Khaosod EnglishYanin’s interest in hornbills began during a primary school field trip to Khao Yai National Park. Fascinated by the birds, she later learned more about the threats affecting their survival and began working towards a solution. The result was ‘Homes for Hornbills,’ a project built around the idea of creating durable artificial nesting spaces from upcycled materials, including discarded plastic bottles. The initiative was developed in collaboration with the ‘Thailand Hornbill Research Foundation’ and goes beyond simply placing artificial nests in forests.The wider conservation model has three main parts. Providing nests designed around hornbill behaviour, teaching students about conservation and developing long-term ways to work with communities in order to reduce pressures such as poaching and deforestation. The idea addresses a particularly important problem for hornbills. The Nation explained that, unlike many birds, hornbills cannot simply build their own nests. They depend on naturally formed cavities in large trees for breeding. As forests disappear and human activity alters their habitats, these suitable nesting sites are becoming increasingly difficult to find.Artificial nests are not entirely new, but Yanin’s project sought to improve on some of the problems associated with existing designs. As per The Nation, traditional wooden nests can deteriorate within 2-3 years and require additional timber. Earthen jar nests may provide limited internal space, potentially restricting the movement and development of young birds. Fibreglass composite nests can last longer, but their glass fibres may also raise concerns about possible irritation over time. Homes for Hornbills therefore explored a different approach. ‘Discarded plastic bottles’ were transformed into resin-based materials, while natural fibres were used instead of conventional glass fibres.Yanin worked with researchers from the Thailand Hornbill Research Foundation to refine important features of the nests, including their size, ventilation, durability and safety for the birds. The project also received support from TOA Venture Holding’s polymer laboratory, where different natural fibres were tested. According to The Nation, hemp showed particularly strong performance during testing because of its ability to absorb the material effectively and resist bending. After adjustments to the fibre mixture and the plastic-based material, the resulting nests were designed to be durable enough to remain functional for up to 10 years.The project has moved beyond the testing stage and into the field. The Nation reported that ‘20 artificial nests’ have been installed on Yao Noi Island in southern Thailand. The early results have been encouraging. During the 2025 breeding season, 10 nests were occupied and 14 hornbill chicks successfully fledged. Khaosod English described the project as involving local students and community members, showing that the initiative is intended to create wider participation rather than operate solely as a scientific experiment. 60 local students had become involved in the project. The next stage is expected to expand the effort further. The Nation reported plans to install 10 large artificial nests in protected forest areas. Yanin has also been raising funds to support the installation of additional nests in ‘Su-ngai Padi National Park’ in Narathiwat province, which provides habitat for endangered hornbill species, including the Helmeted Hornbill and Rhinoceros Hornbill.For Yanin, conservation does not end once an artificial nest is placed in a tree. The initiative also works with children and young people to explain the role hornbills play in forest ecosystems. Hornbills help disperse seeds, making them important to forest regeneration and biodiversity. Yanin has also used storytelling to spread awareness. According to Khaosod English, she produced the documentary ‘Homes for Hornbills,’ which ranked among Thailand’s top 10 youth documentaries. Her project shows how a conservation idea can begin with a simple observation that ‘a bird needs a safe place to breed, while plastic waste needs a better destination than the rubbish bin.’ By connecting those two problems, the 17-year-old has created a solution that has already helped hornbills and brought international attention to the challenges they face. More importantly, Homes for Hornbills demonstrates that meaningful conservation work does not always have to begin with a large organisation or decades of experience. Sometimes, it can start with an idea to make something that can actually be used in the forest.
Article Summary: Thai student Yanin ‘Proud’ Tangkaravakoon has turned a concern for endangered hornbills into a unique conservation project that gives discarded waste plastic a new purpose. Her initiative, ‘Homes for Hornbills’ creates artificial nests designed to provide breeding spaces for hornbill as natural tree cavities become harder to find. The project has now earned her two major international honours, including recognition from ‘The Earth Prize’ and National Geographic’s ‘Slingshot Challenge’

Article Title: In 2015, Florida scientists poured 5 gallons of red dye into Silver River to study how water moved as its clear waters were turning algae-green; they found it took roughly 11.5 hours to travel 5.1 mil
Article Text:
Representation of a dye tracer spreading through a clear spring-fed river, illustrating how scientists can visualise the movement and mixing of water. Image Credits: ChatGPT.

A dye turns invisible movement into a measurable signal

What the tracer revealed about the river

Silver River gorge, near Cadamstown, Co. Offaly. Image Credits: Wikimedia Commons.

Following the river to understand its changing ecology

In 2015, researchers used a fluorescent dye to trace the movement of water through the Silver River, one of Florida’s major spring-fed waterways. The experiment was designed to measure how quickly water travelled through the river, how it mixed along the way and how long it remained in different sections.According to the University of Florida’s Center for Wetlands and Stream Ecosystem Research , the 2015 dye-tracing experiment was part of a broader research effort examining changes in Florida’s spring ecosystems. These included a shift from clear-water conditions dominated by submerged aquatic vegetation towards greater algal growth. Researchers were investigating how changes in river hydraulics and nutrient movement might be related to these ecological changes.On March 8, 2015, researchers from the University of Florida’s Watershed Ecology Lab released five gallons of Rhodamine ET, a red fluorescent dye, at the Main Spring vent in the Silver River. They tracked the dye downstream using nine monitoring stations, including three in-stream fluorometers and six automated samplers. More than 20 student volunteers also collected 318 additional samples overnight. These measurements allowed researchers to calculate the river’s velocity and residence time, referring to how long water remained within the monitored system and its different sections.Fluorescent dye tracing is commonly used to study the movement and mixing of water because the tracer can be detected at successive points along a river.In the Silver River, the method allowed researchers to follow the same water signal downstream rather than relying only on measurements taken at individual locations. The 2015 results showed that the dye travelled the roughly 5.1-mile monitored reach in about 11.5 hours, according to the project’s reported results. That works out to an average travel rate of about 0.44 miles per hour, although the dye did not move at the same rate throughout the river.Researchers later compared the 2015 results with those from another Silver River tracer experiment carried out in 2009. A University of Florida Water Institute study found that the river’s hydraulic behaviour changed under different discharge conditions. At higher discharge, the mean residence time of the spring run decreased, while transient storage increased. In practical terms, this means that changes in river flow can affect both how quickly water travels downstream and how much water temporarily exchanges with slower-moving areas along the channel. Such changes can, in turn, influence how nutrients and other substances move through the river.The researchers were also examining whether these hydraulic conditions were related to differences in algal biomass. Initial findings from the University of Florida showed a negative correlation between water velocity and algal cover in benthic and periphytic habitats. The tracer experiments therefore provided a way to examine the physical conditions alongside the biological observations. Where water moves faster, organisms experience different flow conditions than in areas where water remains longer. These differences can affect the transport and retention of nutrients and other substances, helping researchers examine how changes in river flow may be associated with changes in the river’s biological communities.The Silver River experiment formed part of a larger three-year interdisciplinary research project funded by the St Johns River Water Management District. Ten University of Florida researchers from four departments contributed to the programme, which examined the causes of ecological change in Florida’s springs and possible responses. The tracer experiment focused on how water moved through the Silver River, providing measurements that helped researchers understand the physical conditions within the spring system.The tracer data were also used to calibrate and validate a model of water movement and dye transport through the river. By tracking the tracer from the spring vent downstream, researchers were able to measure how quickly it travelled through different sections of the river and compare those observations with the model's predictions. This provided a more detailed picture of water movement through the system and helped place the biological changes observed in the river within their underlying hydrological conditions.
Article Summary: Researchers used a fluorescent dye to trace the movement of water through the Silver River, one of Florida’s major spring-fed waterways. The experiment was designed to measure how quickly water travelled through the river, how it mixed along the way and how long it remained in different sections. Researchers were investigating how changes in river hydraulics and nutrient movement might be related to these ecological changes.

Article Title: Scotland quarry expansion uncovered a 2,000-year-old woman’s grave; archaeologists were stunned by its carefully built stone walls
Article Text:
'Beautifully made' Iron Age burial site containing the skeleton of a woman at a quarry in Sutherland. Image Credit: Highland Archaeological Services (HAS)

Discovery of the 2,000-year-old unique burial in Scotland

What did the Iron Age grave of a woman look like

Further analysis is being carried out on the grave. Image Credit: Highland Archaeological Services (HAS)

Absence of objects in the women’s grave

What can the skeleton reveal about the woman

A nearly 2,000-year-old carefully constructed stone-lined burial containing the remains of a woman has been discovered at a quarry in Sutherland, Scotland, revealing an unexpected glimpse of life and death at that time. Archaeologists from Highland Archaeological Services(HAS) discovered Evelix, near Dornoch, while carrying out work ahead of a planned quarry expansion. The grave was found within an area where evidence of ancient settlement has also been identified, including features that may once have supported timber roundhouses. What caught the archaeologists’ attention was the unusual quality of the stonework. The structure was so neatly built that, at first, the team wondered whether it could have been modern. Instead, the construction style and archaeological evidence pointed towards the Iron Age, with the woman apparently having remained undisturbed for centuries beneath the ground.The discovery was made during archaeological work connected with the planned expansion of the Evelix quarry near Dornoch. According to the BBC, HAS was working for local quarry firm ‘GF Job’ when archaeologists encountered the stone-lined structure.The location was already considered archaeologically important. The Highland Historic Environment Record shows that the wider Evelix area has produced evidence of prehistoric activity, including burial remains, cremation burials, pottery and features linked to earlier settlement. This newly discovered structure stood out because of its carefully constructed stone lining. Instead of looking like a simple hole dug into the ground, it had been deliberately built with substantial masonry. As per the BBC, archaeologist Lynne McKeggie said the team initially thought the structure might be modern because of how well the stonework had been put together. That first impression quickly changed once the remains and other evidence were examined.The structure was dug into sand and measured approximately 3 metres long, 2 metres wide and 1 metre deep, according to the BBC. A small stone staircase formed part of the construction, adding another feature to the burial. Inside, the remains of an individual were found tucked into one corner. The archaeological team believes the individual was a woman and that she may have lain there undisturbed since the Iron Age. The careful construction is one of the most striking parts of the discovery. The stonework had been fitted together so neatly that the archaeologists described the structure as ‘beautifully made.’ Its appearance raises questions about why so much effort was put into creating it.The Highland Historic Environment Record provides an important background to the discovery. The people who built the structure were working without modern machinery, yet they created a substantial stone-lined space with a staircase. The result survived beneath the landscape for roughly two millennia before quarry-related archaeological work exposed it. Earlier archaeological work at the Evelix quarry area had already shown that the landscape contained evidence of prehistoric activity.The burial does not appear to have contained a collection of obvious grave goods. The BBC reported that no objects were found inside the structure, although archaeologists did identify a large quantity of animal bone. The absence of objects does not make the discovery less significant. In fact, it leaves more questions about the purpose of the structure and the circumstances surrounding the woman's burial. The animal remains may provide useful evidence as further analysis takes place. The construction itself can offer clues about the importance of the site to the people who used it. The wider archaeological record for Evelix also shows that prehistoric burials and settlement activity had previously occurred in the area.The remains could eventually provide a much more personal picture of the woman who was buried at the site. BBC reports that GF Job is funding further analysis of the human remains. Specialists will study the skeleton in greater detail, with the aim of learning more about the individual and the circumstances surrounding the burial. For now, many details remain unknown. Her exact age, background and life story cannot be established simply from the discovery itself. Those answers will depend on the scientific examination still to come. Archaeologists are using photographs and 3D scans to preserve information about the structure and the position of the remains.Once the further analysis has been carried out, the skeleton will be made available to Treasure Trove Scotland for potential allocation to a museum. What began as archaeological work ahead of a modern quarry expansion has revealed a carefully constructed resting place that had remained hidden for around 2,000 years. The woman's identity may never be known, but the grave itself has survived as a quiet reminder of the care and effort that people in Iron Age Sutherland could invest in remembering their dead.
Article Summary: Archaeologists from Highland Archaeological Services(HAS) discovered Evelix, near Dornoch, while carrying out work ahead of a planned quarry expansion. The structure was dug into sand and measured approximately 3 metres long, 2 metres wide and 1 metre deep. Inside, the remains of an individual were found tucked into one corner. Archaeologists believe the individual was a woman and that she may have lain there undisturbed since the Iron Age.

Article Title: In 2024, England turned old fishing nets into a 16-metre footbridge; the 3.5-tonne structure needs smaller foundations and less maintenance than a conventional bridge
Article Text:
The project used modular blocks, which mostly can be placed by hand, instead of traditional reinforced-concrete retaining walls. The blocks fit together like a Lego system, with little or no mortar needed.

Lego-like construction system

A journey by land and sea

Lower carbon footprint, less maintenance

Old fishing nets seldom find a second life. But in Kent, England, the nets are being turned into something much more ambitious. The used nets have been transformed to make a 16-metre-long footbridge to carry people over a marina entrance with minimal environmental impact during construction. Media reports from 2024 say that the Environment Agency built an innovative bridge at Twyford Marina in Yalding using recycled materials, lightweight engineering, and a construction method to reduce the amount of concrete used. The 16-metre bridge is part of the Medway Valley Walk and offers pedestrians a new route across the entrance to Twyford Marina. It also makes it easier for boats to enter and leave the marina. The bridge deck and main structure are made of fibre-reinforced polymer, or FRP, from recycled old fishing nets. The material is a blend of strength and light weight and is particularly useful in a challenging construction location. According to reports, the completed bridge is much lighter at 3.5 tons than many traditional structures of a similar size. The weight reduction also allowed engineers to use smaller support foundations.The innovation is not only the bridge itself. If we go by the GOV UK website, the project used modular blocks, which mostly can be placed by hand, instead of traditional reinforced-concrete retaining walls. The blocks fit together like a Lego system, with little or no mortar needed. According to experts, this method requires less reinforced concrete, making construction simpler and potentially reducing the project's carbon footprint. Lighter materials and smaller footings also allowed the bridge to be constructed in a site where it would have been difficult to deliver large construction equipment.The bridge's journey to Kent was no less strange. According to the GOV UK website, the deck was built in the Netherlands before being shipped to Nottinghamshire and fitted with handrails. From there, the 3.5-ton structure was transported by road to Yalding. Her last voyage was by barge up the River Medway. When the bridge reached the marina, a crane set it in place. The bridge is now open to the public.According to the 2024 report, the Environment Agency anticipates that the recycled FRP structure will require less maintenance than a conventional bridge built from traditional materials. It’s also lighter, which means the foundations it needs are smaller. Less construction material is required, and fewer emissions are generated. In the current scenario, the project shows how infrastructure is a place where pragmatic engineering and the circular economy meet. The project has given a new lease of life to discarded fishing nets, giving them a useful second life in a structure designed to serve walkers and boat users for years. On an ordinary journey, you now pass through an extraordinary piece of environmental engineering at Twyford Marina, made from waste that once belonged to the sea.What are your views on this? Tell us in the comments section below.Images Courtesy: GOV UK and istock
Article Summary: 16-metre-long footbridge made from old fishing nets in Kent, England. Bridge deck and main structure are made of fibre-reinforced polymer, or FRP, from recycled old nets. Modular blocks, which mostly can be placed by hand, instead of traditional reinforced-concrete retaining walls.

Article Title: Nominee vs legal heir: What is the difference and who has claim on assets? All you need to know
Article Text:
AI image

Who is a Nominee?



Who is a Legal Heir?

Difference between a Nominee and a Legal heir

Aspect Nominee Legal Heir Role Custodian Owner Transfer of Assets Can be done without any legal formalities. Requires testamentary documents for proof of ownership. Powers No power to transact, use, or transfer assets. Power to use and transact assets as an owner. Appointment Owner can appoint anyone, but some institutions specify certain conditions. Determined by succession/personal laws. Legal Right Cannot contest ownership legally. Can contest ownership in a court of law.

When individuals open bank accounts, invest in mutual funds, or buy insurance, they are often asked to name a nominee.However, many people mistakenly assume that the nominee automatically inherits the assets. In reality, the nominee is not always the final recipient — the ownership rights belong to the legal heir, reported ET.Understanding the distinction between these two is essential to ensure that your wealth is passed on to the intended beneficiaries.A nominee acts as a temporary custodian of the deceased person’s assets.The nominee’s role is limited to holding and managing the assets until they are legally transferred to the rightful heirs.According to ET, the nominee cannot sell, trade, or make any transactional decisions about the assets.The account or policy owner can appoint anyone — family, friends, or acquaintances — as a nominee, though financial institutions often prefer close family members.In some cases, the nominee and the legal heir can be the same person, which helps in ensuring a smoother transfer of assets.The legal heir or beneficiary is the rightful owner of the assets once the original holder passes away.To claim ownership, the legal heir must produce valid documents such as a will or other testamentary proof.If there is no will — a situation known as dying intestate — the heir is determined as per the country’s succession or personal laws, reported ET.While a nominee can initially access the assets, only the legal heir can claim them permanently or challenge ownership in court.Experts quoted by ET emphasise that having clarity on this difference helps avoid disputes and ensures that the savings reach the intended family members or beneficiaries.Therefore, it is advisable to regularly update both nominees and wills to align with one’s estate planning goals.
Article Summary: A nominee acts as a temporary custodian of the deceased person’s assets. The legal heir or beneficiary is the rightful owner of the assets once the original holder passes away. To claim ownership, the legal heir must produce valid documents such as a will.

How Jeevan Pramaan simplifies pensioner verification



Every year, lakhs of pensioners across India must prove that they are still alive to continue receiving their pension. This verification, known as the Life Certificate or Digital Life Certificate (DLC), is a crucial and mandatory step in ensuring that pension payments are made only to eligible recipients, preventing fraud and misuse.Traditionally, this process involved visiting the bank or pension office in person, standing in long queues, and submitting a signed paper certificate. However, with the government’s focus on digitisation and technological advancement, this process has become much simpler, faster, and more convenient. Pensioners can now submit their certificates digitally from the comfort of their homes using Jeevan Pramaan, a secure, user-friendly, and Aadhaar-based platform.A Life Certificate is an official document that confirms a pensioner is alive. Without it, pension payments are automatically paused by the pension disbursing agency. This verification is essential for preventing fraudulent claims and ensuring that pensions reach the rightful beneficiaries.The Digital Life Certificate (DLC), also known as Jeevan Pramaan, is an advanced biometric-enabled version of the traditional paper certificate.Introduced by the Government of India, it uses Aadhaar-based biometric authentication using either fingerprint or iris scan to verify a pensioner’s identity. Once verified, a digital certificate is automatically generated and shared with authorised pension disbursing agencies.This online process eliminates the need for physical verification, providing elderly pensioners with a simpler and more accessible way to maintain their pension benefits.According to PIB, The submission of the Life Certificate is mandatory for all pensioners who wish to continue receiving their pension without interruption. For the year 2025, the standard submission period is betweenTo make the process more comfortable for the elderly, the government allows pensioners aged 80 years and above to begin the submission process earlier, from 1 October 2025. This extended window gives senior citizens more time and flexibility to complete the procedure without facing last-minute difficulties.The Jeevan Pramaan process involves two main steps: registering the biometric device and generating the digital certificate.Before using the service, pensioners or operators must register their biometric device such as a fingerprint or iris scanner. During registration, the user provides their Aadhaar number and mobile number, after which an OTP (One-Time Password) is sent to their mobile. After entering the OTP, they must provide their name and email ID before scanning their fingerprint or iris.Once authentication is complete, the system confirms that device registration was successful, allowing the user to move to the next step.In this step, the pensioner enters personal details such as Aadhaar number, mobile number, name, PPO number, pension type, sanctioning authority, disbursing agency, and bank account details. The system also asks whether the pensioner has remarried or is re-employed.After entering all details, the pensioner scans their fingerprint or iris using the registered biometric device. Upon successful authentication, the Digital Life Certificate is generated, and an SMS acknowledgment with the Jeevan Pramaan Certificate ID is sent to the registered mobile number.This certificate is automatically stored in the Life Certificate Repository, accessible anytime to both pensioners and pension agencies.Once the Digital Life Certificate is created, it can be electronically delivered to the concerned Pension Disbursing Agency (PDA). PDAs can log in to the Jeevan Pramaan portal to view, verify, or download the certificate directly.Pensioners can also download a PDF copy of their certificate by visiting the Jeevan Pramaan website and entering their Pramaan ID or Aadhaar number. This ensures transparency and easy access for future reference.The government provides several options to submit the Life Certificate, allowing pensioners to choose the method that suits them best.Pensioners who prefer traditional methods can visit their bank branch or a Citizen Service Centre (CSC) to submit their Life Certificate physically. Trained staff at these centres assist pensioners in verifying their details and completing the process.For those unable to travel due to age or health issues, India Post Payments Bank (IPPB) offers a doorstep banking service. Pensioners can schedule an appointment, and an IPPB representative will visit their home to complete the submission using biometric authentication. This service is available for both IPPB and non-IPPB account holders.For pensioners comfortable with technology, the Jeevan Pramaan portal provides a completely online process. By visiting https://jeevanpramaan.gov.in, pensioners can submit their Digital Life Certificate using a computer, laptop, or smartphone equipped with a fingerprint or iris scanner.The system uses the Aadhaar platform to authenticate biometric details. Once verification is successful, a Digital Life Certificate is generated and stored in a secure online repository. Pension disbursing agencies can then directly access the certificate, removing the need for physical paperwork.The UMANG (Unified Mobile Application for New-age Governance) app offers another easy option. Pensioners can download the app from the Google Play Store, search for “Jeevan Pramaan,” and select “Generate Life Certificate.”After entering the necessary details such as Aadhaar number, PPO number, and type of pension, pensioners must authenticate themselves using biometric verification. The app then generates a Digital Life Certificate (DLC), which is automatically shared with the pension disbursing authority.All pensioners who receive government, defence, or private sector pensions through authorised disbursing agencies are required to submit their Life Certificate every year. This includes:Failure to submit the certificate within the stipulated period may result in temporary suspension of pension payments until verification is completed.To ensure a smooth submission process, pensioners should keep certain details and documents ready. These include:Having these details ready helps to avoid delays or errors during authentication, whether submitting online or offline.Yes, an Aadhaar number or Virtual ID (VID) is mandatory to generate a Digital Life Certificate. The entire Jeevan Pramaan system is based on Aadhaar authentication, which ensures accuracy and prevents fraud. Pensioners must make sure their Aadhaar is linked with their mobile number and bank account before attempting to generate the certificate.The Digital Life Certificate is fully valid and legally recognised under the Information Technology Act. Pension disbursing authorities across India accept it as an official document, equivalent to the traditional paper-based life certificate.Its biometric verification system makes it secure and tamper-proof, reducing the chances of wrongful pension disbursal or misuse of pension funds.Before the introduction of Jeevan Pramaan, pensioners often faced difficulties in submitting their certificates, especially those with health problems or limited mobility. The digital system has removed these challenges, allowing pensioners to submit their verification anytime and anywhere.By integrating biometric technology and Aadhaar authentication, Jeevan Pramaan has streamlined pension management, improving efficiency for both pensioners and government departments. It also enhances transparency and ensures that genuine beneficiaries receive payments on time.
Article Summary: A Life Certificate is an official document that confirms a pensioner is alive. Without it, pension payments are automatically paused by the pension disbursing agency. This verification is essential for preventing fraudulent claims and ensuring that pensions reach the rightful beneficiaries. The Digital Life Certificate (DLC), also known as Jeevan Pramaan, is an advanced biometric- enabled version of the traditional paper certificate.

Article Title: How to get your CIBIL credit score without a PAN card
Article Text:
Your credit score is a three-digit number that reflects your creditworthiness and repayment capacity.

What is a CIBIL score?

How to get your CIBIL Credit score without a PAN Card

Factors affecting your CIBIL score

CIBIL credit score : Understanding your creditworthiness is pivotal in today's financial landscape, especially when seeking loans or credit cards. The Credit Information Bureau (India) Limited, commonly known as CIBIL, plays an important role in this regard by providing credit scores to borrowers.According to ET, credit score helps banks make informed decisions about extending credit cards and loans. Your credit history influences your CIBIL score , which is calculated using a special method.Your CIBIL score is a three-digit number that reflects your creditworthiness and repayment capacity. Ranging from 300 to 900, a higher score indicates a stronger likelihood of loan approval. Banks and financial institutions use this score to assess the risk associated with lending money.1. Go to the official CIBIL website and click on 'Personal CIBIL score,' then 'Get Your Free CIBIL score.' Follow the link provided and fill in all the required details.2. If you don’t have a PAN Card, you can use an alternative identification such as Passport, Voter ID, Driver’s License, or Ration Card. Enter the number of the chosen ID.3. Provide your date of birth, PIN code, and select your state. Finally, enter your mobile number and click on ‘Accept and Continue’.4. Authenticate your identity by entering the OTP (One-Time Password) delivered to your mobile device on the next screen. Click 'Continue' to proceed.5. Choose whether you want to link the device with your account. Select 'Yes' or 'No' based on your preference.6. Upon successful registration, you will see a page confirming that 'You have successfully registered!'7. Click on ‘Go to Dashboard’ to access and view your CIBIL score.The factors influencing the new CIBIL score, as stated on the CIBIL website, include:1. Depth of credit: This refers to the duration of your existing credit history, calculated from the opening date of your oldest credit account.2. Long-term trend of outstanding balances: The overall trend of outstanding balances over time affects your score.3. Transaction history on credit cards: How you manage transactions on your credit cards impacts your score.4. Ratio of actual repayment amount to total amount due: This ratio indicates your repayment behavior and influences your score accordingly.5. Number of new accounts opened and number of accounts closed: Opening or closing accounts can affect your score, so managing these actions wisely is important.

Article Title: Meta AI chief Alexandr Wang said that he is willing to wait to have kids till Elon Musk’s Neuralink ...
Article Text:
Why Alexandr Wang wants to wait for Neuralink before having kids

Why Alexandr Wang believes children could adapt better

Alexandr Wang, Meta’s AI chief and highest paid employee, has said he is willing to wait to have children until brain-computer interfaces such as Elon Musk’s Neuralink become more advanced. Wang made the comments during an appearance on the Shawn Ryan Show last year while discussing the future of AI, human development and brain-computer interfaces. He said he wants to wait until Neuralink or similar technology “start working” before having kids. “I want to wait to have kids until we figure out how Neuralink or other … start working,” Alexandr Wang said during the podcast.Wang’s reason is linked to how he believes children’s brains could adapt to the technology. During the podcast, he explained that the first several years of a child’s life are an important period for brain development. He argued that the high level of neuroplasticity during childhood could allow children who grow up with brain-computer interfaces to use the technology in ways that adults may not be able to.“In your first like seven years of life, your brain is more neuroplastic than at any other point in your life, like by an order of magnitude,” Wang said.He then compared the idea with how children develop their ability to process information from their senses.Alexandr Wang described a case involving children born with cataracts. He said that if the cataracts prevent a child from seeing during the early years of development, removing them later may not allow the child to develop normal vision because the brain did not learn to process signals from the eyes during the key period.His view is that a similar effect could eventually apply to brain-computer interfaces. “When we get Neuralink and we get these other technologies, kids who are born with them are going to learn how to use them in like, crazy, crazy ways,” Wang said.Wang said a brain-computer interface could eventually become integrated into the way a person's brain works if it is introduced early enough. He believes this could be different for adults who receive an implant later in life.“It'll be a actually like a part of their brain in a way that it'll never be true for an adult who gets like a neural link or whatever, hooked into their brain,” he said.The Meta AI chief also connected his thinking about brain-computer interfaces to the rapid development of artificial intelligence. “I believe a lot in AI,” Wang said, adding that he expects AI to become “smarter and smarter, more and more capable, more and more powerful.”He said AI could eventually take different forms, including robots and other systems.
Article Summary: Alexandr Wang, Meta’s AI chief and highest paid employee, has said he is willing to wait to have children until brain-computer interfaces become more advanced. Wang made the comments during an appearance on the Shawn Ryan Show last year. He said he wants to wait until Neuralink or similar technology “start working” before having kids.

Google has officially introduced two models under Gemini 3.8, calling it the company's strongest coding and logical reasoning model to date as the company continues a rapid deployment cycle that marks its third Flash launch in six weeks. The latest models arrive three weeks after the debut of version 3.7 Flash, the new release matches the high processing speeds and low cost of its predecessor while branching out into two distinct editions: a general-purpose workhorse model and a specialised cybersecurity release.According to Google, both these models share a common intelligent foundation strengthened by iterative training in cybersecurity, enhanced by recursive agentic loops that continually assess and sharpen performance.Designed for complex, multi-stage reasoning, software development, and autonomous agent workflows, the standard Gemini 3.8 Flash delivers a major step up from version 3.7 while keeping initial pricing fixed at $0.75 per million input tokens and $3.75 per million output tokens, Google says.“Today we’re introducing a new 3.8 Flash model, our 3rd Flash release in just 6 wks. It delivers significant leaps from 3.7 Flash across software engineering, agentic tasks, and multi-step reasoning.On DeepSWE v1.1, it outperforms most larger frontier models in autonomously solving complex engineering problems end to end, at a fraction of the cost,” said CEO Sundar Pichai in a post on X.As per the company, Gemini 3.8 Flash managed to surpass most larger frontier AI systems at a much lower cost on the DeepSWE v1.1 evaluation test, which measures end-to-end software engineering capabilities over extended tasks.The second variant, Gemini 3.8 Flash Cyber, is tailored directly for defensive digital security teams and is being distributed to verified defenders through Google's newly unveiled Fairwind Program. Google emphasised that development for the Cyber model focused heavily on vulnerability remediation rather than offensive exploitation techniques.“We’re also introducing Gemini 3.8 Flash Cyber, our most capable cybersecurity model. It shows frontier-level performance in discovering vulnerabilities and patching them at scale, with Flash-level speed & pricing. That includes achieving 86.2% on the important CyberGym industry benchmark, plus 47.2% on CWE-Bench for patching. We saw a 70%+ success rate in discovering vulnerabilities across 20 programming languages on our internal benchmark,” Pichai said in a separate post.On the same benchmarks, Anthropic’s Opus 5 and GPT-5.6 Sol scored 83.8% and 83.6%, respectively.Google says it has already integrated Gemini 3.8 Flash Cyber into active production defenses. Testing by Google's Chrome Security division revealed that the model generated 2.6 times more accurate vulnerability patches for the Chrome browser than the top commercial models of much larger scale.“Beyond benchmarks, we’re seeing impressive real-world use cases. For example, in evaluations on real Chrome security bugs, 3.8 Flash Cyber produced 2.6x more correct patches for vulnerabilities than larger models. Because of its advanced capabilities, we're giving Government agencies & cybersecurity partners access through the Fairwind program,” Pichai added.
Article Summary: Google has officially introduced two models under Gemini 3.8, calling it the company's strongest coding and logical reasoning model to date. The latest models arrive three weeks after the debut of version 3.7 Flash. The new release matches the high processing speeds and low cost of its predecessor while branching out into two distinct editions: a workhorse model and a specialised cybersecurity release.
